request.prompt:
You are clustering code review findings from the same PR. For each PAIR below, decide whether the two findings describe the SAME underlying issue — same root cause in the same code location. Different wording is fine. A finding about a DIFFERENT defect in the same file or function is NOT the same issue. Severity or aspect differences of the same root cause ARE the same issue.


For THIS scoring pass, duplicate equivalence is stricter than sharing a root cause.
You must compare the COMPLETE MATERIAL CLAIMS, including mechanism, triggering
conditions, execution path, and consequence. The same line or broad concern does
not establish equivalence. A report of wrong-category selection, a case/rename
mismatch, a crash, and a silent fallback are different claims even at one lookup.
An inactive/unbound API concern and an alleged active user-facing failure differ.
A compound report with an additional material claim does NOT equal its subset.
Differences only in wording, severity, or hedging do not create separate claims.
If the claimed mechanisms, triggers or consequences conflict, or one report adds
an unsupported/different material factual claim, return same=false. You are NOT
verifying which claim is true; do not repair or reinterpret either report to make
them match. If unsure whether their full claims are equivalent, return false.

For every numbered pair, extract what A and B actually CLAIM into mechanism,
trigger and consequence. Then list material_differences and give your equivalence
verdict, confidence and reason. same=true requires no material differences.
Return ONLY this JSON object, with EVERY pair index exactly once:
{"pairs":[{"pair":1,"a":{"mechanism":"...","trigger":"...","consequence":"..."},"b":{"mechanism":"...","trigger":"...","consequence":"..."},"material_differences":[],"same":true,"confidence":0.9,"reason":"..."}]}

PAIR 1:
A: The fetch to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends no authentication header, no Content-Type, and no timeout or error handling; the sync response is also a parallel hand-maintained contract with the webhook handler on the other side, with no shared schema as a single source of truth. Any operator who exposes the sync endpoint (as .env.example instructs) has an unauthenticated POST accepting calcomUserId/appSlug; and because the request/response shape exists only as comments in two files, the next edit to one side (e.g. adding the webhook secret header) drifts silently from the other, failing at runtime only during a live token refresh in a booking flow.
B: The sync-endpoint fetch sends no authentication of any kind (no secret, no header) and consumes the response as plaintext tokens, while the inbound webhook path encrypts the same keys with AES-256. Anyone who can reach CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT can POST {calcomUserId, appSlug} and receive live OAuth access tokens for arbitrary users, and the tokens cross the wire with no application-layer encryption — contradicting the confidentiality posture the inbound encryption establishes.

PAIR 2:
A: The findFirst-then-create/update sequence has no concurrency guard or idempotency key, so two in-flight deliveries of the same webhook both take the create branch. A webhook retried while the first delivery is still in flight (senders retry on timeout and this handler has no dedup) creates duplicate (userId, appId) credential rows; later findFirst returns an arbitrary row, so updates can land on a different credential than the one the app reads, leaving stale keys flapping.
B: The findFirst-then-create sequence runs without a transaction and Credential has no unique constraint on (userId, appId), so two concurrent syncs both take the create path, and the unordered findFirst thereafter updates a nondeterministic row. Overlapping initial syncs create duplicate credentials for the same user and app, and later syncs update only one of them, leaving a stale credential that booking flows can still select - producing intermittent 401s that survive every re-sync.

B: The webhook implements create-or-update as a findFirst followed by create/update with no transaction and no unique constraint on Credential(userId, appId), so two concurrent deliveries for the same user+app both miss in findFirst and both execute create. A: The function name and parameter promise schema-pluggability but in sharing mode the caller-provided schema is discarded entirely (minimumTokenResponseSchema wins), a parallel hidden branch that contradicts the signature contract `parseRefreshTokenResponse(response, schema)`. The next developer adding expiry/refresh_token validation to a per-app schema will see their validation silently ignored on shared deployments, and failures that the schema would have caught (missing expiry) pass green while the stored credential is unusable — a stand-in guard that goes green while the real contract is broken.

PAIR 8:
A: The handler resolves reqBody.userId — the calling instance's user id — directly against the local user table with no cross-instance identity mapping or scoping beyond the shared secret. On any deployment whose local user ids do not mirror the parent's id space, synced credentials are attached to an unrelated local user, so that user's bookings and meetings silently route through a stranger's calendar/video account.
B: The handler trusts the parent's raw numeric userId to identify the local user (the schema comment says 'UserId of the cal.com user') with no cross-instance identity mapping or verification such as an email check. Unless the child instance's user id space is kept identical to cal.com's, the webhook delivers one cal.com user's OAuth credentials to the local user holding the same numeric id — a different person — who then books meetings through another user's calendar; any user created or deleted on either side diverges the id spaces and nothing in the design detects it.
